## F420 — LOW — MCP client has no Protected Resource Metadata verification primitive (Wave 334)

**Renumber note:** filed as F419 by wave-334 lane 3; RENUMBERED F419->F420 at the wave-334 merge per the wave-272 earliest-filed rule (lane 2 filed F419 at 04:36:27 UTC, lane 3 at 04:37:31 UTC). Lane 2's F419 (MCP server-side bearer-token gate) keeps the number.

**Cells:** wave-334 lane 3 (RFC 9728 PRM), claim 2026-10-05.

The tree had no Protected Resource Metadata verification at all: tree-wide grep found no `oauth-protected-resource`, no `authorization_servers`, no PRM handling in `gov/`. A resource's PRM document (RFC 9728 section 3.2) was never cross-checked against the sealed authorization-server binding, so an integrator following RFC 9728 for AS discovery -- read the PRM, pick `authorization_servers[0]`, including via a section 5.2 `WWW-Authenticate: resource_metadata` rotation -- could be steered to an attacker AS, and a mismatched `resource` value was never refused. There was no code path taking `(sealed_binding, prm_document)`; the contradiction was silent by absence. Reproduced: `/tmp/red_prm.py` on base `a40c2ef4` -- the forged PRM (attacker AS + mismatched resource) is consumable with no gov/ refusal available.

**Close-when:** a PRM verification primitive exists (`gov/mcp_prm.py`): well-known URL derivation (section 3.1), SSRF-guarded fetch via a deployment-supplied fetcher (section 7.7, never implicit network), `resource` equality against the deployment-configured identifier (section 3.3, mismatch refuses coded `mcp-oauth-prm-resource-mismatched`), `authorization_servers` cross-checked against the sealed binding's issuer (section 4/7.6, omission of the bound issuer refuses coded `mcp-oauth-prm-issuer-unlisted`), `WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata` parsing (section 5.1, same-origin enforced); the red script's forged PRM now refuses coded; regression battery `evals/w334_prm_probes.py` green.

**Severity rationale:** LOW. The gap is integrator-facing: our own OAuth choke points never consumed PRM, so no in-tree bypass existed -- but RFC 9728 is a spec MUST for clients, and without a verified primitive every integrator had to choose between spec compliance (unverified PRM) and security (ignoring PRM). F415/F416/F417 precedent: a loud-by-absence gap requiring an additional misuse step.

**Status: CLOSED 2026-10-05 wave-334 lane 3.** New `gov/mcp_prm.py` (+6 `mcp-oauth-prm-*` codes centrally registered, pin 2077 -> 2083): `derive_prm_url`, `check_prm_url` (https-only, no userinfo/fragment, special-IP literals refused, same-origin enforced), `parse_challenge_resource_metadata`, `verify_prm_document` (shape validation per RFC 9728 section 2/3.2, `resource` equality, `authorization_servers` vs sealed binding via new `mcp_oauth_binding.bound_issuer`), `fetch_prm_document` (deployment-supplied fetcher only; None refuses fail-closed), `discover_and_verify_prm` end-to-end. F417-class bare-ValueError on non-numeric ports is contained at this seam (coded `mcp-oauth-prm-malformed`); F417 itself (OPEN, against `_normalize_url`) is not closed here. `evals/w334_prm_probes.py` 0 BREAK green. No other gov/ changes.

## F421 — MEDIUM — RefreshTokenStore.refresh check-then-set race allows refresh-token double-spend (Wave 335)

**Cells:** wave-335 lane 3 (refresh-token race-guard lock), claim 2026-10-05.

`RefreshTokenStore.refresh` (gov/agent_identity.py) checked `rec["rotated"]` and then, with NO lock, called `normalize_claims` + `issuer.issue()` before setting `rec["rotated"] = True`. Under a threaded/async server two concurrent `refresh` calls against the same (id, secret) both passed the `rotated` check before either set it: one refresh token minted TWO identity tokens plus TWO live refresh chains, and the designed theft response (reuse detection -> whole-chain revocation) never fired because no reuse was ever observed. Reproduced deterministically on base `0fd4f736`: /tmp/red_rtlock.py aligns two threads on a barrier and models a production remote/KMS-backed signer (the tree ships gov/kms_vault.py) with a 0.2s `issuer.issue()`; 3/3 runs: 2/2 refreshes succeeded, both descendant chains live (double-spend). Single-threaded deployments are unaffected; the window is the GIL-released signing call, so any deployment with a slow signer widens it to milliseconds.

**Close-when:** the check-then-set is serialized by per-token locks (not a global lock): concurrent double-refresh yields exactly one success and the loser is refused coded (the existing `identity-refresh-reuse-detected` path, which also revokes the chain); lock acquisition itself is bounded (timeout) and a timeout refuses fail-closed with a new coded outcome instead of proceeding unlocked; sequential and single-threaded behavior unchanged.

**Severity rationale:** MEDIUM. Preconditions are real but narrow: the attacker must already hold the token secret AND achieve concurrency. The consequence defeats a designed security control -- the reuse-detection/chain-revocation theft response never fires, so a racing thief and the legitimate client both walk away with live chains. Any deployment with a remote signer (a supported configuration) widens the window from microseconds to milliseconds.

**Status: CLOSED 2026-10-05 wave-335 lane 3.** Per-token rotation locks in `RefreshTokenStore` (gov/agent_identity.py): `refresh` serializes the rotated-flag check-then-set under the token's own lock (a registry guard mints per-token locks; the guard is never held while acquiring a token lock, so no lock-ordering deadlock); lock acquisition is bounded (5s default, constructor-injectable) and a timeout refuses fail-closed with the new coded outcome `identity-refresh-lock-unavailable` (centrally registered, pin 2100 -> 2101) instead of proceeding unlocked; `_revoke_chain` iterates a snapshot so a concurrent mint cannot raise RuntimeError. The /tmp/red_rtlock.py double-spend now yields exactly one success with the loser refused coded `identity-refresh-reuse-detected` (chain revoked, the existing theft response); regression battery `evals/w335_rtlock_probes.py` 0 BREAK green; `tests/test_dex_identity.py` still green. No other gov/ changes.

## F423 — LOW — PRM URL entry points admit raw ASCII control characters instead of refusing coded (Wave 335)

**F423 (filed 2026-10-05, wave-335 lane 5 as F421; RENUMBERED F421->F423 at the wave-335 merge per the wave-272 earliest-filed rule (lane 3 filed F421 at 05:13:21 UTC, lane 2 at 05:17:38 UTC)).**

**Cells:** wave-335 lane 5 (independent red team), claim 2026-10-05.

`gov/mcp_prm.py`'s URL entry points (`check_prm_url`, `derive_prm_url`, `parse_challenge_resource_metadata`) validate attacker-influenced URLs -- notably the `WWW-Authenticate: resource_metadata` challenge value, which a MITM or rogue server controls -- but never reject ASCII control characters. Two behaviors observed on base `0fd4f736`:

1. `\r`, `\n`, `\t` are silently stripped by `urlsplit` *before* validation, so the "validated" URL is a mutated copy of the wire value: a challenge advertising `https://mcp.example.com/oauth-protected-resource\r\n.evil` is ACCEPTED and normalized to `https://mcp.example.com/oauth-protected-resource.evil` -- the validator blesses a URL that never appeared on the wire.
2. Every other control character (NUL `\x00`, `\x01`--`\x08`, `\x0b`, `\x0c`, `\x0e`--`\x1f`, `\x7f`) is preserved verbatim in the "validated" URL: `check_prm_url("https://mcp.example.com/a\x00b", ...)` ACCEPTS with the NUL intact. A deployment feeding that URL to a standard HTTP client gets an *uncoded* `InvalidURL: URL can't contain control characters` -- the exact F417-class defect (an uncoded exception escaping a seam that promised coded refusal), one layer downstream of validation.

Fail-closed in effect: the sealed binding still governs `verify_prm_document`, the origin check holds (a NUL-bearing host never matches the deployment origin), and no authorization decision is bypassed. The defect is the broken shape contract: a URL that passed `check_prm_url` is not safe to hand to an HTTP client, and a caller catching only the coded error type sees an unexpected exception from a "validated" value.

**Close-when:** `check_prm_url`, `derive_prm_url`, and `parse_challenge_resource_metadata` refuse coded `mcp-oauth-prm-malformed` when the raw URL contains any ASCII control character (0x00-0x1f, 0x7f), checked before `urlsplit` touches it (so CR/LF/TAB refuse instead of being silently stripped); the NUL and CRLF break cases both refuse coded; regression coverage in the wave-335 red-team battery.

**Severity rationale:** LOW. F415/F416/F417 precedent: a coded-shape discipline violation on attacker-influenced input that fails closed in practice -- no bypass, no data leak, but a "validated" URL that a standard HTTP client rejects with an uncoded exception, plus a silent wire-value mutation for CR/LF/TAB.

**Status: CLOSED 2026-10-05 wave-336 lane 1.** Closure evidence: `gov/mcp_prm.py` gained `_reject_control_chars`, called first in `_raw_url_guards` before `urlsplit` touches the value, so every ASCII control character (0x00-0x1f, 0x7f) in a raw PRM-controlled URL refuses coded `mcp-oauth-prm-malformed` on all three entry points (`check_prm_url`, `derive_prm_url`, `parse_challenge_resource_metadata`); the /tmp/red_f423.py break-first repro (6 shapes: CRLF/CR/LF/TAB-strip mutation, NUL/DEL verbatim acceptance) now refuses coded 6/6; `evals/w336_f423_probes.py` 0 BREAK green. No new codes; pin unchanged 2106.

## F424 — LOW — RefreshTokenStore lock_timeout_seconds is unvalidated: NaN escapes refresh() uncoded, negative voids the documented acquisition bound (Wave 336)

**F424 (filed 2026-10-05, wave-336 lane 5 (independent red team)).**

**Cells:** wave-336 lane 5 (independent red team), claim 2026-10-05.

`RefreshTokenStore.__init__` (`gov/agent_identity.py`) accepts `lock_timeout_seconds` with a bare `float(...)` coercion and no validation, although the F421 docstring promises lock acquisition is "bounded (5s default ...); it never proceeds unlocked" and the refusal path is coded (`identity-refresh-lock-unavailable`). Two break cases on base `c4acf39e`:

1. `lock_timeout_seconds=float("nan")`: `threading.Lock.acquire(timeout=nan)` raises bare `ValueError: Invalid value NaN (not a number)`, which escapes `refresh()` UNCODED -- the exact F417-class defect (an uncoded exception from a seam whose contract is coded refusal). Reproduced: `RefreshTokenStore(lock_timeout_seconds=float("nan"))`, mint, `refresh()` -> `ValueError`, not `IdentityTokenRejection`.
2. `lock_timeout_seconds=-1`: the constructor stores `-1.0`; `lock.acquire(timeout=-1)` blocks FOREVER under contention, silently voiding the documented bound. Reproduced: hold the token's lock on the main thread, call `refresh()` on a worker with the store at `-1` -> the worker never returns (daemon thread + 4s join observed the hang). In the F421 theft scenario (legitimate client racing a stolen secret) the loser hangs forever leaking a thread instead of receiving the coded `identity-refresh-lock-unavailable` refusal, and the reuse-detection theft response never fires for it.

Fail-closed in the safety sense (the hang blocks rather than refreshing unlocked), but the liveness bound the module documents is voided by a plausible deployment value (`-1` is the widespread "no timeout" convention), and the NaN shape is an uncoded exception on a coded seam.

**Close-when:** `RefreshTokenStore.__init__` validates `lock_timeout_seconds`: must be a finite number >= 0 (NaN/inf/negative refused at construction, fail-closed); the two break cases refuse/raise coded or at construction; regression coverage in the wave-336 red-team battery (P3e).

**Severity rationale:** LOW. Deployment-config-gated (not agent-reachable), liveness-only, and the safety property (never refresh unlocked) still holds. F415/F416/F417 precedent: a discipline violation on a documented bound with an uncoded escape on one shape.

**Status: CLOSED 2026-10-05 wave-337 lane 1.** Closure evidence: `RefreshTokenStore.__init__` (`gov/agent_identity.py`) now validates `lock_timeout_seconds` at construction via `_validate_lock_timeout` (must be a finite number >= 0; NaN/inf/negative/non-numeric refuse with ValueError, fail-fast at deployment time); timeout 0 documented as one non-blocking acquire attempt (still the coded `identity-refresh-lock-unavailable` refusal when contended); the /var/tmp/g337-red.py break-first repro confirmed both shapes RED on base 2f270987 and the constructor now refuses them before any refresh can run; `evals/w337_f424f425_probes.py` 0 BREAK green (9 construction-validation probes incl. zero/non-blocking semantics and default-bound regression). No new codes; pin unchanged 2106.

## F425 — LOW — Executor per-tool rate-limiter fail-closed path crashes uncoded on wire failure (Wave 336)

**F425 (filed 2026-10-05, wave-336 lane 5 (independent red team)).**

**Cells:** wave-336 lane 5 (independent red team), claim 2026-10-05.

`Executor._check_tool_rate` (`gov/executor.py`) documents: "any unexpected exception from the wire becomes a coded `tool-rate-limiter-unavailable` denial -- a broken limiter denies, never allows unlimited." The `except Exception` handler sets the coded denial, but then calls `self._tool_rate_wire.windowed_count(tool)` to fill the diagnostic refusal record -- and `windowed_count()` re-invokes the broken clock (`self._clock()` inside `_evict`). **Status: CLOSED 2026-10-05 wave-337 lane 1.** Closure evidence: `Executor._check_tool_rate` (`gov/executor.py`) now guards the diagnostic `windowed_count()` against the same unexpected-exception class, so it can never re-invoke a broken wire and mask the coded denial with an uncoded escape; on a broken wire the chained refusal record carries `rate_windowed_count=None` (unfit to count) and the caller always sees coded `tool-rate-limiter-unavailable`; the /var/tmp/g337-red.py break-first repro confirmed the raw-escape shape RED on base 2f270987 and the denial now arrives coded with its chained record; `evals/w337_f424f425_probes.py` 0 BREAK green (limiter-failure coded-denial + record probes, plus exceeded-path and approved-sweep regressions unchanged). **F427 (filed 2026-10-05, wave-339 lane 5 (continuous real-model attack)).**

2. A `delete_file` call through `g` returns `allow` with `output_info["framework_tool"] == "read_file"`, while direct `binding.call("delete_file", ...)` for the same caller is `denied` ("Role 'support' is not allowed to use tool 'delete_file'") -- the same role-policy bypass as F426, on a certified agent, on the F426-closed tree.

The F426 close-when ("rejects missing or mismatched attachment") is satisfied literally -- the guardrail declares a name, and the name matches -- but "mismatched attachment" in the hazard sense (guardrail built for a different tool) is not rejected when the declaration agrees with the attachment. The declaration is the operator's claim about the wiring; the audit verifies the claim is present and spelled right, never that it is true.

**Close-when:** `audit_agent_coverage` verifies the guardrail's `framework_tool` against a deployment-declared SDK-tool-name -> framework-tool mapping (new parameter, e.g. `sdk_tool_map`), rather than trusting the operator-supplied `expect_sdk_tool_name` string alone: a tool is certified only when at least one issued guardrail satisfies BOTH `expect_sdk_tool_name == <sdk tool name>` AND `framework_tool == sdk_tool_map[<sdk tool name>]`; tools with no mapping entry, or guardrails whose `framework_tool` disagrees with the mapping, are uncovered surfaces (`UncoveredSurfaceError`). Deployments that cannot declare the mapping must treat SDK tools as uncovered rather than certifying on the declaration alone. Regression: the F427 break shape refuses at audit, the honest construction (mapping-consistent) still certifies, and the declared-name-mismatch shape still refuses.

**Severity rationale:** LOW. Same class as F426: deployment-misconfiguration, not agent-reachable (the deployer must construct the guardrail with the mismatched pair). But the audit's purpose is catching wiring mistakes, and the F426 closure re-opens the identical bypass for any declaration that agrees with the attachment -- the check verifies the declaration's spelling, not its truth.

**Status: CLOSED 2026-10-05 wave-340 lane 1.** `audit_agent_coverage` now takes a deployment-declared `sdk_tool_map` (SDK tool name -> framework tool name) and verifies the guardrail's `framework_tool` against it: a tool is certified only when at least one issued guardrail satisfies BOTH `expect_sdk_tool_name == <sdk tool name>` AND `framework_tool == sdk_tool_map[<sdk tool name>]`. Tools with no mapping entry, guardrails whose `framework_tool` disagrees with the mapping, and any issued guardrail declaring this SDK tool's name while mediating a different framework tool (declared-name lie present on the tool, including the two-guardrail shape) are uncovered surfaces (`UncoveredSurfaceError`); deployments that cannot declare the mapping (`sdk_tool_map=None`) treat every SDK tool as uncovered rather than certifying on the declaration alone. New `coverage_drift(report, agent)` names post-audit tool-set drift (openai-agents #5124: the SDK resolves tools after agent start hooks). Red-first verified: the F427 break shape (read_file guardrail declaring delete_file on the delete_file tool) refuses at audit, the honest mapping-consistent construction still certifies, and the declared-name-mismatch shape still refuses. ## F426 — LOW — audit_agent_coverage certifies guardrail<->tool misattachment: calls mediated under the wrong tool's policy (Wave 337)

**F426 (filed 2026-10-05, wave-337 lane 4 (independent red team)).**

**Cells:** wave-337 lane 4 (independent red team), claim 2026-10-05.

`audit_agent_coverage` (`gov/adapters/openai_agents.py`) certifies an SDK `Agent` as fully covered when every `FunctionTool` carries "one of this module's issued guardrails" -- but it never checks that the guardrail was built for THAT tool. The issued guardrail function does not expose the `framework_tool` it mediates (`expect_sdk_tool_name` is only a closure variable), so the audit cannot verify the correspondence even in principle.

Break proof on base `2f270987` (support role: `read_file` allowed, `delete_file` denied by role policy):
1. Build an agent whose single FunctionTool `delete_file` carries the guardrail built by `make_tool_input_guardrail(binding, "read_file")` -> `audit_agent_coverage` returns success (certified).
2. A `delete_file` call through the misattached guardrail returns `allow` with `output_info["framework_tool"] == "read_file"` and decision `executed`, while the direct `binding.call("delete_file", ...)` for the same caller is `denied` ("Role 'support' is not allowed to use tool 'delete_file'"). In the real SDK flow the guardrail's `allow` lets the SDK invoke the `delete_file` implementation -- a role-policy bypass on a certified agent.
3. Second shape (F417-class on the guardrail seam): a `write_file` guardrail attached to the `send_email` FunctionTool (coder) -- the arg-shape mismatch makes the executor simulation raise a bare `KeyError: 'path'` that escapes the guardrail function UNCODED. In the real SDK this crashes the run (fail-closed, no execution) but the coded-refusal contract is broken exactly on the miswired path.

The `expect_sdk_tool_name` parameter exists precisely because misattachment is a known hazard, but it is optional, and the audit never consults it.

**Close-when:** the issued guardrail function exposes the `framework_tool` it mediates and its declared `expect_sdk_tool_name` as attributes; `audit_agent_coverage` raises `UncoveredSurfaceError` for any FunctionTool whose attached issued guardrail declares no `expect_sdk_tool_name` or declares one that does not equal the SDK tool's name; regression coverage in the wave-337 red-team battery (P3a).

**Severity rationale:** LOW. Deployment-misconfiguration class (not agent-reachable): the deployer must attach the wrong guardrail. But the audit's whole purpose is catching wiring mistakes, and it certifies exactly this one -- including the allow-direction bypass above.

**Status: CLOSED 2026-10-05 wave-338 lane 1.** The issued guardrail now exposes `framework_tool` and `expect_sdk_tool_name` as attributes; `audit_agent_coverage` raises `UncoveredSurfaceError` for any FunctionTool whose issued guardrail declares no `expect_sdk_tool_name` or declares one that does not equal the SDK tool's name (both break shapes now refuse at audit); arg-shape access is wrapped so a bare `KeyError` from mediation refuses coded `guardrail_argument_shape_mismatch` via the tripwire instead of escaping uncoded. Red-first verified on the base tree for all three break shapes; no new decision codes, pin unchanged 2124; `evals/w338_f426_probes.py` 0 BREAK green.
